text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Moderate party leader Carl Bildt says the new accord between Russia and NATO means a fresh risk that Sweden will be marginalised in future discussions on peace and security in the region. Sweden, therefore, must step up its cooperation with the 16 member defence alliance, Bildt says.
- Fire risks are continuing in forests throughout Sweden due to a hot, dry spell. On Sunday bushfires destroyed large areas of forest in south Norrland and Gothenburg.

- The words of Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson do not count anymore, the paper said. Sweden has lost influence in the European Union since the ruling party stated its views on Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU). Last week the ruling Social Democrats said the country should not join EMU in 1999 but left the door open to join at a later date.

- The world's largest lock company, Assa Abloy, has bought Czech lock company FAB which could lead to more business in eastern Europe. The company also bought Elsafe, the largest manufacturer of hotel room safes, through its subsidiary Vingcard. Assa Abloy managing director Carl-Henrik Svanberg said in an interview that high criminality in Russia could also benefit the company.

- Foreign ambassadors and trade agencies are approaching Swedish companies who have expressed interest in moving their headquarters abroad. Clothing retailer Hennes & Mauritz, for example, has been approached by representatives from Ireland, Britain and The Netherlands.

- Mobile telephone company Allgon's incoming managing Torsten Korsell says sales of mobile telephone handsets will increase fivefold to 100 million by the year 2000, a higher forecast than the company said earlier. But he said the company must improve its relationship with telecoms group AB LM Ericsson in order to meet this goal.
